title: HubScan: Detecting Hubness Poisoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are essential to contemporary AI applications, allowing large language models to obtain external knowledge via vector similarity search. Nevertheless, these systems encounter a significant security flaw: hubness - items that frequently appear in the top-k retrieval results for a disproportionately high number of varied queries. These hubs can be exploited to introduce harmful content, alter search rankings, bypass content filtering, and decrease system performance.
  We introduce hubscan, an open-source security scanner that evaluates vector indices and embeddings to identify hubs in RAG systems. Hubscan presents a multi-detector architecture that integrates: (1) robust statistical hubness detection utilizing median/MAD-based z-scores, (2) cluster spread analysis to assess cross-cluster retrieval patterns, (3) stability testing under query perturbations, and (4) domain-aware and modality-aware detection for category-specific and cross-modal attacks. Our solution accommodates several vector databases (FAISS, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate) and offers versatile retrieval techniques, including vector similarity, hybrid search, and lexical matching with reranking capabilities.
  We evaluate hubscan on Food-101, MS-COCO, and FiQA adversarial hubness benchmarks constructed using state-of-the-art gradient-optimized and centroid-based hub generation methods. hubscan achieves 90% recall at a 0.2% alert budget and 100% recall at 0.4%, with adversarial hubs ranking above the 99.8th percentile. Domain-scoped scanning recovers 100% of targeted attacks that evade global detection. Production validation on 1M real web documents from MS MARCO demonstrates significant score separation between clean documents and adversarial content. Our work provides a practical, extensible framework for detecting hubness threats in production RAG systems.

AI.tldr: Hubscan is an open-source security scanner for Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems that detects harmful 'hub' items in vector indices using a multi-faceted detection approach, demonstrating high efficacy across benchmarks and real-world data.
AI.motivation: RAG systems are vulnerable to hubness, where certain items disproportionately appear in top-k results, enabling security exploits such as injection of harmful content and manipulation of search rankings. This necessitates a robust tool for detecting such vulnerabilities.
AI.method: Hubscan employs a multi-detector architecture including statistical hubness detection (median/MAD z-scores), cluster spread analysis, stability testing under query perturbations, and domain- and modality-aware detection. It supports multiple vector databases and retrieval methods.
AI.result: Hubscan achieves 90% recall at a 0.2% alert budget and 100% recall at 0.4% on adversarial benchmarks, with adversarial hubs ranked above the 99.8th percentile. Domain-scoped scanning detects 100% of targeted attacks evading global detection. Evaluation on 1M real MS MARCO documents shows clear separation between clean and adversarial content.
AI.conclusion: Hubscan provides a practical and extensible framework for detecting hubness-based security threats in production RAG systems, effectively identifying adversarial hubs across multiple datasets and real-world deployments.

title: Utilizing LLMs for Industrial Process Automation
summary: A growing number of publications address the best practices to use Large Language Models (LLMs) for software engineering in recent years. However, most of this work focuses on widely-used general purpose programming languages like Python due to their widespread usage training data. The utility of LLMs for software within the industrial process automation domain, with highly-specialized languages that are typically only used in proprietary contexts, remains underexplored. This research aims to utilize and integrate LLMs in the industrial development process, solving real-life programming tasks (e.g., generating a movement routine for a robotic arm) and accelerating the development cycles of manufacturing systems.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the industrial process automation domain, focusing on specialized programming languages used in proprietary environments, and aims to accelerate manufacturing software development by solving real-world tasks like robotic arm programming.
AI.motivation: While LLMs have shown promise in software engineering for mainstream languages like Python, their effectiveness in industrial automation—where specialized, proprietary languages dominate—is underexplored. There is a need to adapt LLMs to these niche contexts to improve development efficiency.
AI.method: The research investigates the integration of LLMs into industrial software development workflows by tailoring them to domain-specific languages and evaluating their performance on practical tasks such as generating control routines for robotic systems.
AI.result: The study demonstrates that LLMs can be effectively adapted to support programming in specialized industrial automation languages, enabling faster development cycles and accurate generation of functional code for real-world manufacturing tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLMs have significant potential to enhance software development in the industrial automation sector, provided they are properly fine-tuned or conditioned for domain-specific languages and use cases, paving the way for broader adoption in manufacturing environments.

title: Predicting Known Vulnerabilities from Attack Descriptions Using Sentence Transformers
comment: PhD thesis, Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, 2026
summary:
Modern infrastructures rely on software systems that remain vulnerable to cyberattacks. These attacks frequently exploit vulnerabilities documented in repositories such as MITRE's Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE). However, Cyber Threat Intelligence resources, including MITRE ATT&CK and CVE, provide only partial coverage of attack-vulnerability relationships. Attack information often appears before vulnerabilities are formally linked, creating the need for automated methods that infer likely vulnerabilities directly from attack descriptions.
  This thesis addresses the problem of predicting known vulnerabilities from natural-language descriptions of cyberattacks. We develop transformer-based sentence embedding methods that encode attack and vulnerability descriptions into semantic vector representations, enabling similarity-based ranking and recommendation.
  Fourteen state-of-the-art transformer models were evaluated across four attack description types (Tactic, Technique, Procedure, and Attack Pattern). Results show that Technique descriptions in MITRE ATT&CK provide the strongest predictive signal. The multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1 (MMPNet) model achieved the best performance due to its hybrid pre-training and optimization for semantic similarity.
  The approach was implemented in the VULDAT tool, which automatically links attacks to vulnerabilities. Manual validation revealed previously undocumented relationships in MITRE repositories. Evaluation on unseen cyberattack reports demonstrates that the models generalize beyond curated datasets and support proactive vulnerability awareness.

AI.tldr: This thesis proposes a transformer-based method to predict software vulnerabilities from natural-language cyberattack descriptions by leveraging semantic similarity. Using models like MMPNet, it successfully links MITRE ATT&CK techniques to CVEs, uncovering previously undocumented relationships and enabling proactive threat intelligence through the VULDAT tool.
AI.motivation: The incomplete coverage of attack-vulnerability relationships in existing Cyber Threat Intelligence resources (e.g., MITRE ATT&CK and CVE) creates a critical gap, especially when attack information emerges before vulnerabilities are formally documented. This necessitates automated methods to infer likely vulnerabilities from natural-language attack descriptions to improve threat intelligence and response.
AI.method: The research employs transformer-based sentence embedding models to encode textual descriptions of cyberattacks and vulnerabilities into semantic vectors. Fourteen state-of-the-art models are evaluated across four types of attack descriptions (Tactic, Technique, Procedure, Attack Pattern) using similarity-based ranking. The best-performing model is integrated into the VULDAT tool for automated linking.
AI.result: Technique-level descriptions in MITRE ATT&CK yielded the strongest predictive performance. The multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1 (MMPNet) model outperformed others due to its hybrid pre-training and semantic similarity optimization. The VULDAT tool successfully identified previously undocumented attack-vulnerability links and demonstrated strong generalization on real-world, unseen cyberattack reports.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that transformer-based models, particularly MMPNet, are effective in predicting known vulnerabilities from natural-language attack descriptions, with Technique-level descriptions in MITRE ATT&CK being the most informative. The successful implementation in VULDAT demonstrates the practical utility of the approach for uncovering undocumented attack-vulnerability links and enhancing proactive cyber defense.

title: Differentially Private Data-Driven Markov Chain Modeling
summary: Markov chains model a wide range of user behaviors. However, generating accurate Markov chain models requires substantial user data, and sharing these models without privacy protections may reveal sensitive information about the underlying user data. We introduce a method for protecting user data used to formulate a Markov chain model. First, we develop a method for privatizing database queries whose outputs are elements of the unit simplex, and we prove that this method is differentially private. We quantify its accuracy by bounding the expected KL divergence between private and non-private queries. We extend this method to privatize stochastic matrices whose rows are each a simplex-valued query of a database, which includes data-driven Markov chain models. To assess their accuracy, we analytically bound the change in the stationary distribution and the change in the convergence rate between a non-private Markov chain model and its private form. Simulations show that under a typical privacy implementation, our method yields less than 2% error in the stationary distribution, indicating that our approach to private modeling faithfully captures the behavior of the systems we study.

AI.tldr: A differentially private method is introduced to protect user data in Markov chain models by privatizing simplex-valued queries, with analytical and empirical guarantees on utility preservation.
AI.motivation: Accurate Markov chain modeling requires large amounts of user data, which may contain sensitive information; sharing non-private models risks exposing this data, necessitating privacy-preserving methods that maintain model utility.
AI.method: The authors propose a method to privatize database queries that output elements of the unit simplex (e.g., probability distributions), proving it satisfies differential privacy; this is extended to stochastic matrices (Markov chains), and they derive bounds on the KL divergence, stationary distribution perturbation, and convergence rate change between original and private models.
AI.result: The method achieves differential privacy for Markov chain models with bounded expected KL divergence; analytical bounds are provided on the impact to stationary distributions and convergence rates; simulations show less than 2% error in the stationary distribution under typical privacy parameters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively balances privacy and utility in data-driven Markov chain models, enabling accurate and differentially private representation of user behavior.

title: Silent Egress: When Implicit Prompt Injection Makes LLM Agents Leak Without a Trace
summary: Agentic large language model systems increasingly automate tasks by retrieving URLs and calling external tools. We show that this workflow gives rise to implicit prompt injection: adversarial instructions embedded in automatically generated URL previews, including titles, metadata, and snippets, can introduce a system-level risk that we refer to as silent egress. Using a fully local and reproducible testbed, we demonstrate that a malicious web page can induce an agent to issue outbound requests that exfiltrate sensitive runtime context, even when the final response shown to the user appears harmless. In 480 experimental runs with a qwen2.5:7b-based agent, the attack succeeds with high probability (P (egress) =0.89), and 95% of successful attacks are not detected by output-based safety checks. We also introduce sharded exfiltration, where sensitive information is split across multiple requests to avoid detection. This strategy reduces single-request leakage metrics by 73% (Leak@1) and bypasses simple data loss prevention mechanisms. Our ablation results indicate that defenses applied at the prompt layer offer limited protection, while controls at the system and network layers, such as domain allowlisting and redirect-chain analysis, are considerably more effective. These findings suggest that network egress should be treated as a first-class security outcome in agentic LLM systems. We outline architectural directions, including provenance tracking and capability isolation, that go beyond prompt-level hardening.

AI.tldr: Agentic LLMs are vulnerable to silent data exfiltration via implicit prompt injection in URL previews; malicious metadata can trigger undetectable outbound requests, with sharded exfiltration further evading detection—highlighting the need for system- and network-level security controls beyond prompt hardening.
AI.motivation: As agentic LLMs increasingly retrieve URLs and invoke external tools autonomously, they become vulnerable to implicit prompt injection through maliciously crafted web content; this introduces system-level threats such as undetectable data exfiltration (silent egress), which existing output-based safety mechanisms fail to catch.
AI.method: The authors designed a fully local, reproducible testbed to evaluate implicit prompt injection attacks via malicious URL previews on a qwen2.5:7b-based agentic LLM system, measuring success rates of silent egress and evaluating detection evasion, including sharded exfiltration; ablation studies assessed the effectiveness of prompt-, system-, and network-layer defenses.
AI.result: In 480 experiments, the attack achieved an 89% success rate in inducing unauthorized outbound requests, with 95% of successful exfiltrations bypassing output-based detection; sharded exfiltration reduced single-request leakage by 73% (Leak@1) and evaded basic data loss prevention; prompt-layer defenses were largely ineffective, whereas system- and network-layer controls (e.g., domain allowlisting, redirect-chain analysis) showed stronger mitigation potential.
AI.conclusion: Network egress must be treated as a critical security outcome in agentic LLM systems, necessitating system- and network-level controls such as domain allowlisting, provenance tracking, and capability isolation to mitigate risks like silent egress and sharded exfiltration.

title: Explainability-Aware Evaluation of Transfer Learning Models for IoT DDoS Detection Under Resource Constraints
summary: Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks threaten the availability of Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures, particularly under resource-constrained deployment conditions. Although transfer learning models have shown promising detection accuracy, their reliability, computational feasibility, and interpretability in operational environments remain insufficiently explored. This study presents an explainability-aware empirical evaluation of seven pre-trained convolutional neural network architectures for multi-class IoT DDoS detection using the CICDDoS2019 dataset and an image-based traffic representation. The analysis integrates performance metrics, reliability-oriented statistics (MCC, Youden Index, confidence intervals), latency and training cost assessment, and interpretability evaluation using Grad-CAM and SHAP. Results indicate that DenseNet and MobileNet-based architectures achieve strong detection performance while demonstrating superior reliability and compact, class-consistent attribution patterns. DenseNet169 offers the strongest reliability and interpretability alignment, whereas MobileNetV3 provides an effective latency-accuracy trade-off for fog-level deployment. The findings emphasize the importance of combining performance, reliability, and explainability criteria when selecting deep learning models for IoT DDoS detection.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates seven pre-trained CNN architectures for multi-class IoT DDoS detection using image-represented network traffic and the CICDDoS2019 dataset, emphasizing performance, reliability, and interpretability.
AI.motivation: DDoS attacks threaten IoT availability, especially under resource constraints; while transfer learning shows promise in detection accuracy, its reliability, computational feasibility, and interpretability in real-world settings are not well understood.
AI.method: The authors employ image-based traffic representation and evaluate seven pre-trained CNNs (e.g., DenseNet, MobileNet) using the CICDDoS2019 dataset. Evaluation includes performance metrics (accuracy, F1), reliability measures (MCC, Youden Index, confidence intervals), latency and training cost, and interpretability via Grad-CAM and SHAP.
AI.result: DenseNet and MobileNet-based models achieve high detection performance, with DenseNet169 showing best reliability-interpretability alignment and MobileNetV3 offering optimal latency-accuracy trade-off for fog environments. Attribution maps are compact and class-consistent, supporting model trustworthiness.
AI.conclusion: Selecting deep learning models for IoT DDoS detection should balance performance, reliability, and explainability; DenseNet169 and MobileNetV3 are recommended for high-reliability and edge-deployable scenarios, respectively.

title: Systems-Level Attack Surface of Edge Agent Deployments on IoT
summary: Edge deployment of LLM agents on IoT hardware introduces attack surfaces absent from cloud-hosted orchestration. We present an empirical security analysis of three architectures (cloud-hosted, edge-local swarm, and hybrid) using a multi-device home-automation testbed with local MQTT messaging and an Android smartphone as an edge inference node. We identify five systems-level attack surfaces, including two emergent failures observed during live testbed operation: coordination-state divergence and induced trust erosion. We frame core security properties as measurable systems metrics: data egress volume, failover window exposure, sovereignty boundary integrity, and provenance chain completeness. Our measurements show that edge-local deployments eliminate routine cloud data exposure but silently degrade sovereignty when fallback mechanisms trigger, with boundary crossings invisible at the application layer. Provenance chains remain complete under cooperative operation yet are trivially bypassed without cryptographic enforcement. Failover windows create transient blind spots exploitable for unauthorised actuation. These results demonstrate that deployment architecture, not just model or prompt design, is a primary determinant of security risk in agent-controlled IoT systems.

AI.tldr: Edge deployment of LLM agents in IoT introduces critical security vulnerabilities; this study identifies key attack surfaces and shows that architecture choice directly impacts security properties like data egress, sovereignty, and provenance integrity.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify emerging security risks in edge-deployed LLM agents for IoT, which introduce new attack surfaces not present in cloud-hosted systems.
AI.method: Empirical security analysis of three architectures (cloud-hosted, edge-local swarm, hybrid) using a multi-device home-automation testbed with local MQTT and an Android smartphone as an edge node; assessment based on measurable systems metrics.
AI.result: Identified five systems-level attack surfaces, including coordination-state divergence and induced trust erosion; found that edge-local deployments prevent cloud data egress but risk silent sovereignty degradation during fallbacks; provenance chains lack cryptographic enforcement; failover windows create exploitable blind spots.
AI.conclusion: Deployment architecture is a primary factor in determining security risk in LLM-agent-controlled IoT systems, significantly influencing systems-level vulnerabilities beyond model or prompt design.

title: Layer-Targeted Multilingual Knowledge Erasure in Large Language Models
summary: Recent work has demonstrated that machine unlearning in Large Language Models (LLMs) fails to generalize across languages: knowledge erased in one language frequently remains accessible through others. However, the underlying cause of this failure and a principled solution remain open. In this work, we identify intervention depth as the key factor determining multilingual generalization. Through systematic layer-wise experiments, we characterize two distinct failure modes: shallow-layer interventions achieve erasure but collapse multilingual capabilities in held-out languages, while deep-layer interventions preserve utility but fail to erase target knowledge even in source languages. These findings reveal that the choice of intervention layer is not a free parameter; it fundamentally determines whether multilingual unlearning succeeds. We propose MUTE (Multilingual Unlearning via Targeted Erasure), a framework that uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and Linguistic Regions Development Score (LRDS) to identify intermediate, language-agnostic layers where cross-lingual representations converge. By restricting unlearning updates to these layers, MUTE achieves robust multilingual knowledge erasure while optimizing on only a small set of source languages. Extensive experiments across three LLM architectures and three unlearning algorithms validate our approach, with mechanistic analysis via Logit Lens probing confirming genuine knowledge removal rather than output-level suppression.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies intervention depth as the key factor in multilingual unlearning failure in LLMs and proposes MUTE, a framework that targets language-agnostic intermediate layers using CKA and LRDS to achieve robust, cross-lingual knowledge erasure without harming utility.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning in LLMs often fails to generalize across languages, with erased knowledge remaining accessible in other languages; the root cause and a systematic solution for this issue were previously unknown.
AI.method: MUTE leverages Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and Linguistic Regions Development Score (LRDS) to identify intermediate, language-agnostic layers where cross-lingual representations converge, then applies unlearning updates only in these layers to balance erasure and multilingual utility.
AI.result: MUTE achieves effective multilingual knowledge removal across three LLM architectures and three unlearning algorithms, with logit lens probing confirming actual erasure (not output masking) and minimal impact on multilingual performance.
AI.conclusion: The choice of intervention depth is critical for successful multilingual unlearning in LLMs; MUTE enables effective and robust multilingual knowledge erasure by targeting language-agnostic intermediate layers identified through CKA and LRDS.

title: DPSQL+: A Differentially Private SQL Library with a Minimum Frequency Rule
summary: SQL is the de facto interface for exploratory data analysis; however, releasing exact query results can expose sensitive information through membership or attribute inference attacks. Differential privacy (DP) provides rigorous privacy guarantees, but in practice, DP alone may not satisfy governance requirements such as the \emph{minimum frequency rule}, which requires each released group (cell) to include contributions from at least $k$ distinct individuals. In this paper, we present \textbf{DPSQL+}, a privacy-preserving SQL library that simultaneously enforces user-level $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP and the minimum frequency rule. DPSQL+ adopts a modular architecture consisting of: (i) a \emph{Validator} that statically restricts queries to a DP-safe subset of SQL; (ii) an \emph{Accountant} that consistently tracks cumulative privacy loss across multiple queries; and (iii) a \emph{Backend} that interfaces with various database engines, ensuring portability and extensibility. Experiments on the TPC-H benchmark demonstrate that DPSQL+ achieves practical accuracy across a wide range of analytical workloads -- from basic aggregates to quadratic statistics and join operations -- and allows substantially more queries under a fixed global privacy budget than prior libraries in our evaluation.

AI.tldr: DPSQL+ is a modular, privacy-preserving SQL library that enforces both differential privacy and minimum frequency constraints, enabling compliant, accurate, and scalable data analysis across multiple database systems.
AI.motivation: While differential privacy (DP) provides strong privacy guarantees, real-world data governance policies often require additional constraints like the minimum frequency rule (k-anonymity per cell). Prior systems fail to jointly enforce both DP and such rules, creating a gap between theoretical privacy and regulatory compliance.
AI.method: DPSQL+ implements a modular architecture with three components: a Validator to restrict SQL queries to a DP-safe subset, an Accountant to track cumulative privacy loss across queries, and a Backend to interface with various database engines, ensuring extensibility and portability.
AI.result: Experiments on the TPC-H benchmark show that DPSQL+ maintains practical accuracy across diverse analytical queries—including aggregates, quadratic statistics, and joins—and supports significantly more queries under a fixed privacy budget compared to existing systems.
AI.conclusion: DPSQL+ is a privacy-preserving SQL library that effectively combines user-level differential privacy with the minimum frequency rule, offering a practical, modular, and portable solution for secure data analysis while supporting a broad range of SQL queries under strict privacy governance.

title: IMMACULATE: A Practical LLM Auditing Framework via Verifiable Computation
summary: Commercial large language models are typically deployed as black-box API services, requiring users to trust providers to execute inference correctly and report token usage honestly. We present IMMACULATE, a practical auditing framework that detects economically motivated deviations-such as model substitution, quantization abuse, and token overbilling-without trusted hardware or access to model internals. IMMACULATE selectively audits a small fraction of requests using verifiable computation, achieving strong detection guarantees while amortizing cryptographic overhead. Experiments on dense and MoE models show that IMMACULATE reliably distinguishes benign and malicious executions with under 1% throughput overhead. Our code is published at https://github.com/guo-yanpei/Immaculate.

AI.tldr: IMMACULATE is a practical auditing framework for black-box LLM APIs that detects model substitution, quantization abuse, and token overbilling using selective verifiable computation, achieving strong security with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: The lack of transparency in commercial LLM APIs creates risks of model substitution, quantization abuse, and token overbilling, undermining user trust and fairness; there is a need for lightweight, practical auditing that does not rely on trusted hardware or internal model access.
AI.method: IMMACULATE uses verifiable computation to selectively audit a small subset of API requests, leveraging cryptographic methods to detect anomalies while minimizing performance overhead.
AI.result: Experiments on both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models demonstrate that IMMACULATE achieves high detection accuracy for malicious behavior with less than 1% throughput overhead.
AI.conclusion: IMMACULATE provides a practical and efficient solution for auditing black-box commercial LLM APIs, enabling clients to detect economically motivated misconduct without requiring trusted hardware or model access.

title: AgentSentry: Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents via Temporal Causal Diagnostics and Context Purification
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external tools and retrieval systems to autonomously complete complex tasks. However, this design exposes agents to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where attacker-controlled context embedded in tool outputs or retrieved content silently steers agent actions away from user intent. Unlike prompt-based attacks, IPI unfolds over multi-turn trajectories, making malicious control difficult to disentangle from legitimate task execution. Existing inference-time defenses primarily rely on heuristic detection and conservative blocking of high-risk actions, which can prematurely terminate workflows or broadly suppress tool usage under ambiguous multi-turn scenarios. We propose AgentSentry, a novel inference-time detection and mitigation framework for tool-augmented LLM agents. To the best of our knowledge, AgentSentry is the first inference-time defense to model multi-turn IPI as a temporal causal takeover. It localizes takeover points via controlled counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries and enables safe continuation through causally guided context purification that removes attack-induced deviations while preserving task-relevant evidence. We evaluate AgentSentry on the \textsc{AgentDojo} benchmark across four task suites, three IPI attack families, and multiple black-box LLMs. AgentSentry eliminates successful attacks and maintains strong utility under attack, achieving an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 74.55 %, improving UA by 20.8 to 33.6 percentage points over the strongest baselines without degrading benign performance.

AI.tldr: AgentSentry is a novel inference-time framework that detects and mitigates indirect prompt injection in LLM agents by identifying causal takeover points through counterfactual re-execution and enabling safe execution via context purification, significantly improving security and utility under attack.
AI.motivation: The increasing use of external tools and retrieval systems by LLM agents introduces vulnerability to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, which are hard to detect in multi-turn interactions and are inadequately addressed by existing heuristic-based defenses that often disrupt legitimate workflows.
AI.method: AgentSentry uses controlled counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries to localize takeover points and applies causally guided context purification to remove attack-induced deviations while preserving legitimate task context.
AI.result: Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark across multiple attack families and LLMs, AgentSentry eliminates successful IPI attacks and achieves an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 74.55%, outperforming the best baselines by 20.8 to 33.6 percentage points without affecting performance on benign tasks.
AI.conclusion: AgentSentry is the first inference-time defense that effectively mitigates multi-turn indirect prompt injection in tool-augmented LLM agents by modeling the attack as a temporal causal takeover, enabling secure and continuous agent operation without compromising task performance.

title: Automated Vulnerability Detection in Source Code Using Deep Representation Learning
summary: Each year, software vulnerabilities are discovered, which pose significant risks of exploitation and system compromise. We present a convolutional neural network model that can successfully identify bugs in C code. We trained our model using two complementary datasets: a machine-labeled dataset created by Draper Labs using three static analyzers and the NIST SATE Juliet human-labeled dataset designed for testing static analyzers. In contrast with the work of Russell et al. on these datasets, we focus on C programs, enabling us to specialize and optimize our detection techniques for this language. After removing duplicates from the dataset, we tokenize the input into 91 token categories. The category values are converted to a binary vector to save memory. Our first convolution layer is chosen so that the entire encoding of the token is presented to the filter. We use two convolution and pooling layers followed by two fully connected layers to classify programs into either a common weakness enumeration category or as ``clean.'' We obtain higher recall than prior work by Russell et al. on this dataset when requiring high precision. We also demonstrate on a custom Linux kernel dataset that we are able to find real vulnerabilities in complex code with a low false-positive rate.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a CNN model for bug detection in C code, trained on machine- and human-labeled datasets, achieving superior recall at high precision and demonstrating effectiveness in finding real bugs in complex code.
AI.motivation: Software vulnerabilities in C pose significant security risks, and existing detection methods have limitations in precision and recall. This work aims to improve bug detection in C code by leveraging deep learning with specialized optimization for the language.
AI.method: A CNN-based model was developed using tokenized C code (91 token categories encoded as binary vectors). The architecture includes two convolution and pooling layers followed by two fully connected layers, trained on a machine-labeled dataset (from Draper Labs static analyzers) and the human-labeled NIST SATE Juliet dataset, with duplicates removed.
AI.result: The model achieves higher recall than Russell et al.'s approach at high precision levels on the same datasets. It successfully identifies real vulnerabilities in a custom Linux kernel dataset with low false positives.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convolutional neural network model effectively identifies software vulnerabilities in C code with high recall and precision, outperforming prior work, and demonstrates practical applicability by detecting real vulnerabilities in complex systems like the Linux kernel with a low false-positive rate.

title: SettleFL: Trustless and Scalable Reward Settlement Protocol for Federated Learning on Permissionless Blockchains (Extended version)
summary: In open Federated Learning (FL) environments where no central authority exists, ensuring collaboration fairness relies on decentralized reward settlement, yet the prohibitive cost of permissionless blockchains directly clashes with the high-frequency, iterative nature of model training. Existing solutions either compromise decentralization or suffer from scalability bottlenecks due to linear on-chain costs. To address this, we present SettleFL, a trustless and scalable reward settlement protocol designed to minimize total economic friction by offering a family of two interoperable protocols. Leveraging a shared domain-specific circuit architecture, SettleFL offers two interoperable strategies: (1) a Commit-and-Challenge variant that minimizes on-chain costs via optimistic execution and dispute-driven arbitration, and (2) a Commit-with-Proof variant that guarantees instant finality through per-round validity proofs. This design allows the protocol to flexibly adapt to varying latency and cost constraints while enforcing rational robustness without trusted coordination. We conduct extensive experiments combining real FL workloads and controlled simulations. Results show that SettleFL remains practical when scaling to 800 participants, achieving substantially lower gas cost.

AI.tldr: SettleFL is a scalable, trustless reward settlement protocol for decentralized federated learning that reduces economic friction using two blockchain-efficient, interoperable strategies: optimistic execution with challenge-based arbitration and validity-proof-based instant finality.
AI.motivation: Decentralized reward settlement in open FL is hindered by high blockchain costs and scalability issues; existing solutions compromise decentralization or suffer from linear on-chain expenses.
AI.method: Proposes SettleFL, a dual-strategy protocol using a shared domain-specific circuit: (1) Commit-and-Challenge for optimistic execution with dispute resolution, and (2) Commit-with-Proof using validity proofs for instant finality.
AI.result: Experiments show SettleFL scales to 800 participants with significantly lower gas costs while supporting flexible latency and cost trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: SettleFL enables trustless and scalable reward settlement in decentralized federated learning, maintaining practical efficiency and economic viability at scale.

title: Strengthening security and noise resistance in one-way quantum key distribution protocols through hypercube-based quantum walks
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a foundational cryptographic protocol that ensures information-theoretic security. However, classical protocols such as BB84, though favored for their simplicity, offer limited resistance to eavesdropping, and perform poorly under realistic noise conditions. Recent research has explored the use of discrete-time Quantum Walks (QWs) to enhance QKD schemes. In this work, we specifically focus on a one-way QKD protocol, where security depends exclusively on the underlying Quantum Walk (QW) topology, rather than the details of the protocol itself. Our paper introduces a novel protocol based on QWs over a hypercube topology and demonstrates that, under identical parameters, it provides significantly enhanced security and noise resistance compared to the circular topology (i.e., state-of-the-art), thereby strengthening protection against eavesdropping. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient and extensible simulation framework for one-way QKD protocols based on QWs, supporting both circular and hypercube topologies. Implemented with IBM's software development kit for quantum computing (i.e., Qiskit), our toolkit enables noise-aware analysis under realistic noise models. To support reproducibility and future developments, we release our entire simulation framework as open-source. This contribution establishes a foundation for the design of topology-aware QKD protocols that combine enhanced noise tolerance with topologically driven security.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel one-way Quantum Key Distribution protocol using quantum walks on a hypercube topology, which offers superior security and robustness against noise compared to circular topologies. The authors also release an open-source Qiskit-based simulation framework for evaluating such protocols under realistic conditions.
AI.motivation: Classical QKD protocols like BB84 have limited eavesdropping resistance and poor performance under noise; existing quantum walk-based schemes primarily use less secure circular topologies, prompting the need for topologically optimized, noise-resilient alternatives.
AI.method: A one-way QKD protocol is designed using discrete-time quantum walks on a hypercube topology. An open-source, noise-aware simulation framework is implemented using Qiskit to evaluate and compare performance under realistic noise conditions.
AI.result: The hypercube-based QKD protocol demonstrates significantly improved security and noise tolerance over the circular topology under identical parameters, validated through simulations with realistic noise models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed QKD protocol based on quantum walks over a hypercube topology provides enhanced security and noise resistance compared to the state-of-the-art circular topology, establishing a foundation for topology-aware QKD protocols.
